title: Caldera Inference Finance - Console Orientation

Ethan Ross: Export example route-level telemetry CSV and sample dashboard (due 2028-05-18)

summary: AE + SE walkthrough of Redwood Console usage analytics, per-route cost breakdown, and Optimize recommendations. Customer (Caldera) is evaluating hosted vs private for regulated data; key concerns: latency, predictable billing, KMS integration, SOC2 auditability. Agreed to pilot a single inference route with telemetry and cost checks.
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2028-05-14 15:00 PDT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Ross (Redwood SE), Lina Wu (Redwood PM); Dr. Aaron Kim, Priya Nair, Sam Ortiz, Olivia Park (Caldera)

Auto-summary (auto): Quick console tour focused on per-route spend and usage lenses.

[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we can see a full list here — hey Dr. Kim, thanks for making time. We'll run through the console, show per-route dashboards, and then Ethan will jump into the telemetry and the Optimize suggestions.
[00:22] Dr. Aaron Kim: Thanks Maya, hi all. We're mainly evaluating how to get predictable inference costs for our clinical annotation pipelines. We run a mix of long-context and short chat prompts, so curious how Redwood surfaces that.
[00:36] Maya Patel: Totally — quick housekeeping, recording on, chat for links. Ethan, want to take it away on the console?
[00:44] Ethan Ross: Yeah sure, I'll share screen — bear with me while I bring up the routes view. So what you're looking at is the per-route list; each route has a cost-per-token trend, latency percentiles, and a usage lens that breaks down top prompts and token distribution.
[01:12] Priya Nair: Real quick — are you capturing KV cache hits in that lens? We do a lot of prefix reuse so that matters for effective token counts.
[01:25] Ethan Ross: Good call. The panel shows cache hit rate as an overlay (we sometimes label it "KV hits" in the UI), and the cost model reduces billable tokens when cache is used. Small note — the transcription for that metric sometimes shows as "K-V cache" in older exports.
[01:47] Sam Ortiz: On the cost model, is that actual billed amount or a projected estimate? We need something we can reconcile with our finance ops.
[01:58] Lina Wu: The console uses your billing granularity — for hosted it's actual per-token billing; for Dedicated or Private we show allocated GPU cost + infra amortization as an estimated unit cost. We can export raw token events for reconciliation.
[02:21] Olivia Park: Security question — if we go private do we still have the same console telemetry? We need audit logs sent to our SIEM and KMS integration for keys.
[02:34] Maya Patel: Yes, Private includes a customer-controlled control plane option and we stream audit logs. KMS/HSM integrations are supported; Ethan will link the KMS doc.
[02:49] Dr. Aaron Kim: Timeline — we want a pilot in the next two weeks and then a broader POC if the numbers look good. Our compliance window is early Q3 so that drives the cadence.
[03:02] Maya Patel: Great, we'll plan for a 2-week pilot. Ethan, show the route detail page.
[03:10] Ethan Ross: Ok, route detail. On the top you have throughput and latencies P50/P95/P99. Underneath there's a token composition view — prompt tokens, generation tokens, and cached tokens. Notice the blue slices — those are short completions. The cost breakdown is to the right; it shows model unit cost, infra overhead, and applied discounts (if you have reserved capacity).
[03:45] Priya Nair: Do you support mapping routes to internal teams for chargeback? We need route -> cost center mappings and export to our billing system.
[03:57] Ethan Ross: Yes — route metadata supports tags for cost centers and project IDs. Exports can be scheduled daily as CSVs and we have a billing API for push integration.
[04:18] Dr. Aaron Kim: How do rollouts and canaries appear in the console? We do progressive rollouts and we need to compare A/B quality and cost delta.
[04:29] Lina Wu: Rollouts show up as overlays on the route timeline; you can split by variant and compare latency, cost, and quality metrics side-by-side. There's an auto-fallback policy so if latency spikes, traffic automatically moves to the fallback model.
[04:47] Sam Ortiz: About Optimize — can you recommend batching or quantization settings per route? We're trying to reduce per-token spend for bulk annotation jobs.
[05:01] Ethan Ross: That's exactly what Redwood Optimize does. It looks at request size distribution and suggests batching windows, cache TTLs, and quantization profiles — and it will simulate expected cost savings. The recommendations page will show confidence bands; for highly variable long-context requests the suggestion sometimes is to use a different model variant.
[05:22] Priya Nair: I'm concerned about tail latency when batching for throughput. Any tradeoff guidance?
[05:31] Ethan Ross: There's a tradeoff slider in the Optimize UI — you can tune for latency SLO or unit cost. For your latency-sensitive routes, we recommend smaller continuous batches and prefix caching; for batch annotation jobs, larger batches and model quantization.
[05:49] Dr. Aaron Kim: Could you run a simulated run for our typical 8k context doc? We get big KV loads.
[05:58] Maya Patel: We can — action item for Ethan to run a benchmark with your sample prompt set under both hosted and Dedicated configs.
[06:10] Ethan Ross: Yep I'll schedule that. Now drilling into a route's details — here's the top prompt contributors and how much each contributes to tokens. You can pin a prompt set as an 'eval' to surface quality regressions; we tie that to alerts.
[06:34] Olivia Park: On alerts, we need immutable logs for audit. Does the console provide retention TTLs and export to S3?
[06:44] Lina Wu: Yes — you can configure retention on the telemetry side and we support direct S3 log sink and SIEM forwarding. Also note, for Private installs you control retention policies entirely.
[06:57] Sam Ortiz: Pricing — for Reserved/Dedicated, do you show effective per-token costs after amortization? Our CFO will want to see chargeback numbers.
[07:08] Ethan Ross: Dedicated shows amortized GPU cost per token and the console has a 'finance mode' that maps those costs back to routes and tags. We also let you model burst capacity and the cost impact.
[07:25] Dr. Aaron Kim: Any known limits on embedding endpoints vs text generation? We use embeddings for semantic search and another team for chat.
[07:36] Maya Patel: The console separates endpoint types and each route can be configured with a model type — embeddings routes are metered differently and oftentimes cheaper per unit. We can show a combined view or route-by-route.
[07:54] Priya Nair: How about data residency — do we have region locks for logs and model serving? We are in EU as well.
[08:03] Lina Wu: Region pinning is supported for both hosted and Private — you can pin to eu-west or us-west. For Private on-prem you control everything.
[08:15] Ethan Ross: Jumping ahead to the cost decomposition widget — here we break down into model compute, inference kernel overhead, networking, and console analytics storage. Note that for heavy KV loads the model compute dominates, but for many short chat requests analytics storage and calls can be significant.
[08:40] Sam Ortiz: One more billing ask: can we get a daily anomaly detection for spend spikes? We had a rogue job last quarter.
[08:50] Ethan Ross: Yes — there's an anomaly detector. It flags spikes and can send Slack/email or open a ticket in your ticketing system. It also highlights unusual token distributions so you can trace the root prompt.
[09:06] Dr. Aaron Kim: Walk me through an example export — like if we want last 30 days of route events.
[09:14] Ethan Ross: There's an export button; you can filter by tags, route, model, and date range. Exports include timestamp, route ID, prompt tokens, completion tokens, cache flag, model version, and response latency. Small note: older exports labeled model version as 'model hash' in some instances, the UI now shows both.
[09:41] Maya Patel: Quick check — any blockers on your side for pilot?
[09:46] Priya Nair: We need internal sign-off for data egress on hosted. If we must go hosted for pilot, we need a written data handling plan.
[09:57] Olivia Park: And KMS integration for encryption at rest — we need to validate key policies.
[10:04] Maya Patel: We'll send the SOC2 and KMS docs and a short data handling note.
[10:11] Sam Ortiz: On the pilot scope, we'd like to include cost dashboards and daily export. If that works, we can have ops own the pilot.
[10:20] Dr. Aaron Kim: Also include one long-context route and one batch annotation route so we see both extremes.
[10:28] Ethan Ross: Sounds good. On the Optimize side I'll pre-populate recommendations and a simulated cost delta for both routes — will include packing, quantization, and batch sizes.
[10:39] Priya Nair: About the console UI — can we add internal labels that don't leak to Redwood? Like internal project names that stay in our tenant only?
[10:48] Lina Wu: Yes, tags and metadata are tenant-scoped; they won't be visible to other tenants. For Dedicated/Private they are fully under your control.
[10:59] Maya Patel: I'll recap next steps in a follow-up email. Ethan, any other callouts?
[11:06] Ethan Ross: Two callouts — one, when you run the benchmark include a typical KV cache warm-up window as that materially affects cost; two, if you have preference for quantization (int8 vs int4) let us know and we'll include both sims.
[11:21] Sam Ortiz: We currently haven't standardized quantization internally, so both would be useful.
[11:27] Dr. Aaron Kim: Who will own the pilot on Redwood's side?
[11:31] Maya Patel: I'll be the AE. Ethan will handle technical leads and Lina is the product contact for console questions.
[11:39] Olivia Park: Final security note — we will need an on-call for any data incident during pilot; who do we contact?
[11:46] Maya Patel: We'll provide a support escalation doc; for pilots it's our standard SE oncall plus AE escalation. We'll include that in the follow-up.
[11:55] Priya Nair: Cool. Also can you show how the quality alerts tie to eval sets? We want to detect hallucination spikes.
[12:05] Ethan Ross: Sure — here's the eval panel in the console. You can attach a prompt set and a rubric; the quality alerts watch for metric drift and can annotate which prompts caused the regression. Note: hallucination detection is an active area — our labels are heuristics and you can plug in custom eval scripts.
[12:28] Dr. Aaron Kim: That looks helpful. For the pilot we'll supply prompt samples and an 'oracle' for scoring.
[12:35] Maya Patel: Great. We're about halfway through the timebox so let's switch to a quick live demo of setting up a route and enabling the finance mode.
[12:44] Ethan Ross: I'm creating a new route now — name it 'caldera-annotate'. Setting tags to 'team=nlp, cost_center=annotation'. Choosing model family and enabling prefix caching. Now enabling finance mode — you can pick amortization window (monthly, quarterly) and add reserved capacity details.
[13:12] Sam Ortiz: Does the finance model accept our amortization rate? We have internal charges per GPU hour.
[13:21] Ethan Ross: Yup you can input your internal rate or use Redwood's default; the console will compute an effective per-token cost based on average token throughput.
[13:35] Priya Nair: Can we preview the cost change if we toggle quantization?
[13:40] Ethan Ross: Yes — there's a 'what-if' simulator; toggle q4->q8 or int8->int4 and it re-simulates compute time and cost. The sim is best-effort and we recommend running a short benchmark for exact numbers.
[13:56] Dr. Aaron Kim: Any pitfalls you see for us?
[14:01] Maya Patel: Common pitfall is not tagging routes consistently — that'll make chargeback hard. Also, not warming the cache before measuring can understate gains.
[14:12] Ethan Ross: And for Dedicated, misconfiguring autoscale policies can leave you with cold starts that spike latency — we can help define safe autoscale curves.
[14:25] Priya Nair: Ok that helps. For the pilot, Sam will own cost measurement; Priya will own infra and Aaron will be product owner.
[14:35] Maya Patel: Perfect. I'll send a recap with links to the console tour recording, the security packet, and the sample export.
[14:44] Dr. Aaron Kim: Thanks everyone. One last question — if we want on-prem later, what's the rough timeline for transition? We may start hosted and move to Private.
[14:55] Lina Wu: Typical on-prem transition timeline is 6-10 weeks depending on network and compliance packaging; we can run a readiness checklist early.
[15:07] Sam Ortiz: Good. That covers it for me.
[15:12] Maya Patel: Great — thanks all. We'll follow up with the docs and next steps.

End of meeting
